title: Rethinking Forgery Attacks on Semantic Watermarks in Black-Box Settings: A Geometric Distortion Perspective
claim: An adversary can invert a stolen watermarked output through a proxy model and forge content that still passes the provider's watermark check.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right loop; red dashed proxy-model box on right
description: A single wide diagram of the black-box forgery threat model. On the left, a text-to-image service (building icon) wraps a dashed 'Target Model' encoder-decoder shape. A user icon exchanges arrows with a watermarked landscape image. A green check and a red cross mark the verdicts for the original image and the forged image. A dashed arrow labeled 'Steal' carries the watermarked image into a large pink, red-dashed 'Proxy Model' region with a hooded hacker icon. Inside, an encoder E-hat feeds latents z0, zt and zT, shown as orange boxes under an 'Inverse Scheduler' arrow. The zT latent then goes to a 'Forgery Methods' box that lists guidance-based and optimization-based strategies and has a devil icon. A decoder D-hat then outputs a forged image with a watermark droplet. That image returns to the service and is rejected. Red tones draw the eye to the attacker region.
caption: Illustration of the black-box forgery attack. An adversary uses a proxy model to invert a watermarked image into a latent representation and generates a forged image via different strategies, which preserves the service provider's watermark while falsifying content provenance.
abstract: Recent studies have shown that semantic watermarks, which embed information into the initial noise of latent diffusion models (LDMs), are vulnerable to black-box forgery attacks. However, existing methods primarily rely on empirical evidence and lack a rigorous theoretical understanding of the conditions under which such attacks succeed or fail. To bridge this gap, we rethink the nature of such attacks through the lens of rate-distortion in the latent space. Our analysis identifies an irreducible distortion floor due to structural mismatches between proxy and target models, which fundamentally limits the fidelity of forged watermarks. We further characterize this distortion as structured geometric deviations on the latent manifold, in the form of global drift and local deformation rather than stochastic noise. Leveraging these insights, we propose a scheme-agnostic detection method that distinguishes forged samples before watermark verification. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across diverse black-box scenarios, while preserving robustness to common distortions.
